standard.title: Evaluate sources and perspectives
standard.description: evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS5S04 (Evaluate source purpose and perspective): Students can evaluate sources for origin, purpose and perspective, identify bias and stereotypes, and compare accounts from different sources. Students apply a source analysis framework independently.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives, including identifying persuasive techniques, distinguishing fact from opinion, and assessing the relevance and context of sources.

nodes.label: Publication details and content evaluation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine a source's publishing details and content to clarify its purpose, distinguish fact from opinion, identify potential bias, assess its relevance, and contextualise its information.
nodes.minimum_width: For one source, examine publishing details and content to identify purpose, one example of fact vs opinion, and one indicator of potential bias.
nodes.typical_width: For a range of primary and secondary sources, examine publishing details (author, publisher, date, type) and content to: clarify purpose, distinguish fact from opinion, identify potential bias, assess relevance, and place information in historical or geographic context.
wider: Apply a systematic source audit protocol to a set of sources used in an inquiry — document findings for each source and assess how source quality affects inquiry reliability
Investigate how publication date affects interpretation — compare a government report from the 1950s with a contemporary one on the same social topic and explain what has changed and why
nodes.hinge_reason: Source evaluation at Year 6 requires integrating multiple criteria simultaneously — students who evaluate on one criterion only (e.g. just checking for bias) will miss the complex interplay between origin, purpose, content and context that determines usefulness.

response_modes.reason: Use a multi-criteria evaluation frame (purpose / fact vs opinion / bias / relevance / context) applied consistently to each source — the Year 6 challenge is applying all criteria to every source, not just one at a time.

success_criteria: Students examine at least one source using at least three evaluation criteria (purpose, fact/opinion, bias, relevance, context).
Students correctly distinguish at least one fact from one opinion in the source.

nodes.label: Identifying persuasive techniques
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify persuasive techniques in sources, including modality language and passive voice, and explain why writers use these techniques.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one persuasive technique in a source and explain how it is used to shape the reader's view.
nodes.typical_width: Identify persuasive techniques in sources: modality language (would, could, may, might — hedging claims), passive voice ('It is claimed that...' versus active 'The government claims...'), and other techniques — and explain what each technique does and why the writer chose it.
wider: Compare a factual report and a persuasive text on the same HASS topic, identifying all persuasive techniques in the second text and evaluating their effectiveness
Analyse a political speech or campaign material for persuasive techniques and assess how the techniques shape the audience's perception of the issue

response_modes.reason: Modality and passive voice are linguistic concepts that require explicit instruction — model these techniques with annotated examples before students identify them independently.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Analysing political speeches and campaign materials for persuasive technique is a rich media literacy direction that connects to civic knowledge and has genuine transferable value for critical citizenship.
success_criteria: Students identify at least one persuasive technique in a source.
Students explain why the writer used the technique and what effect it has on the reader.

nodes.label: Discussing contested perspectives and proposing reasons
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss issues explored in sources where there were or are a range of views, and propose reasons for why perspectives differ.
nodes.minimum_width: For one contested issue, describe two different perspectives and propose one reason why they differ.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss issues explored through sources where there are or were multiple views (e.g. deportation of South Sea Islanders, women's vote, sustainable environment management, migration) — identify the perspectives represented, explain what each view involves, and propose reasons for why perspectives differ.
wider: Evaluate points of view about a sustainability issue using sources representing producers' and consumers' perspectives, and assess the expertise of each source expressing a view

Investigate a historically contested decision (e.g. deportation of Pacific Islanders, immigration restriction) from multiple perspectives and evaluate which perspective has stronger evidential support

response_modes.reason: Contested perspectives are best understood by comparing multiple different viewpoints — not just 'for and against' but examining what different groups valued and why. Breadth of perspectives is the key enrichment direction.

success_criteria: Students identify at least two perspectives on a contested issue.
Students propose at least one reason why perspectives differ.

nodes.label: Integrated source evaluation across a Year 6 inquiry
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate a range of primary and secondary sources for origin, purpose and perspectives, applying persuasive technique analysis and multi-criteria evaluation to assess each source's usefulness.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate at least two sources using multiple criteria (origin, purpose, perspective, persuasive technique) and assess the usefulness of each for an inquiry.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate a set of primary and secondary sources across a Year 6 inquiry: examine publishing details, distinguish fact from opinion, identify persuasive techniques, assess bias and relevance, consider historical and geographic context, and explain how each source's origin, purpose and perspective affects its usefulness.
wider: Produce a source evaluation report for a Year 6 inquiry that documents findings for each source and explains how source quality influenced the inquiry conclusions
Evaluate a source set for coverage gaps — identify perspectives, time periods or types of evidence that are not represented, and explain how these gaps affect the conclusions that can be drawn

response_modes.reason: Integrated source evaluation at Year 6 requires applying all criteria (origin, purpose, fact/opinion, persuasive technique, relevance, context) simultaneously and making a usefulness judgment. Support with a structured evaluation template.

success_criteria: Students evaluate at least two sources using at least three evaluation criteria each.
Students identify persuasive technique in at least one source.
Students assess each source's usefulness for the inquiry and explain the reasoning.
